Look beneath the total ↓

What does it mean for two countries to have similar refugee policies? In the Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies, Finland and Namibia have almost the same overall index in 2022. Yet the protections recorded inside those totals look quite different.

This is a story about what aggregation hides—and what a score alone cannot establish. These data describe laws and policies on paper. They do not measure a refugee’s experience, implementation, or conditions today.

01

Separate the protections

One total. Five different dimensions.

Read each pair of marks on the same 0–1 scale. The widest separation identifies the field to investigate; it is not that field’s contribution to the overall score.

04

Change the time horizon

A snapshot is only one moment.

Follow the selected pair through the annual data. Step lines preserve the discrete observations. A flat segment means the recorded index stayed the same; it does not establish that nothing changed in people’s lives.

The timeline uses the pair selected in chapter 01. Missing years are gaps, not zeros. Each step occurs at the next recorded year; no change date within that year is inferred.

05

Read the fine print

The evidence trail is part of the story.

How the pairs are chosen

We rank qualifying pairs by their largest absolute field difference, descending; ties use overall difference, then country IDs. Finland–Namibia is an editorial case selected for traceable legal language, not the top-ranked pair.

What the comparison can tell us

Values are the supplied inverse-covariance-weighted (ICW) indices. We do not average the five displayed fields to recreate the total. Short excerpts illustrate selected provisions; they cannot account for an entire weighted field. The full document, population, conditions, and date remain essential.

What we checked

Processing is deterministic and separate from the interface. Source-key uniqueness, score ranges, benchmark exclusions, pair counts, largest-gap calculations, historical observations, and exact generated output are checked before release.

What remains open

Only the featured movement comparison and the Philippines coverage issue have curated documentary evidence in this MVP. Other pairs are leads for further reading. The excerpts do not independently validate every code or prove implementation. No scores have been “corrected” from our reading.

How this builds on existing DWRAP work

The official dashboard already offers country comparisons, field/strand decomposition, trends, distributions, benchmarks, weighting choices, and data downloads. Those capabilities are not our novelty.

Our narrower contribution is a reproducible search for similar totals followed by a curated audit: field difference → raw code → cited clause → scope and version limits. The evidence is allowed to complicate or challenge the numerical story. We have inspected the dashboard’s published interface, not every runtime interaction; we do not claim that legal text is absent from all of its features.

Coverage, missingness, and historical entities

The catalog’s country count differs from the supplied workbook’s entities. We retain the workbook definitions and label the counts explicitly. Historical country names follow the source. No discernible policy can be coded at the low end; zero is not automatically evidence of an explicit prohibition.

Sources, downloads, and reproducibility

Data: World Bank; Christopher W. Blair, Guy Grossman and Jeremy M. Weinstein. 2024. Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies. Supplied workbook and September 2024 Technical Guide. Dataset attribution is retained in the source package.
